docs.title: copper-and-code-mcu-boards
docs.text:
MicroPython and LVGL firmware for microcontroller boards with a touch screen. Flash the board, then import display_driver: the display, the touch and LVGL are running, and the same program works on every board here. Write the GUI in Python, run it with mpremote or Thonny, or design it in Copper and Code Studio and upload it from there.

Download

Ready images for every board in the releases, with their SHA-256 sums.

One driver, every board

WIDTH, HEIGHT, start(), stop(), backlight() and what a Ctrl-C does are the same everywhere: the display_driver contract.

Upstream, unchanged

MicroPython 1.29 and omnipython-lvgl as they are: out-of-tree boards and C modules, no fork.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
1. Download the image for your board from the latest release.
  2. Flash it: the RP2350 takes the .uf2 on its USB drive; the STM32 boards with DFU; the ESP32-4848S040 with esptool.
  3. Run an example:
import display_driver
import lvgl as lv

label = lv.label(lv.screen_active())
label.set_text("Hello")
label.center()

The program can end there: display_driver keeps LVGL running from a timer.

docs.title: The display_driver contract
docs.text:
Every board has a frozen display_driver.py: - python/display_driver.py on the RP2350; - python/stm32/display_driver.py on the STM32H743 boards; - python/esp32/display_driver.py on the ESP32-S3.

The names below are what an application, a test or Copper and Code Studio may rely on, on every board. Everything else in the drivers is internal and may change between releases.

Version 1 (CONTRACT = 1), from firmware v0.1.7. Before it, firmware v0.1.6 and older, there is no CONTRACT.

docs.title: Names
docs.text: Name What it promises import display_driver Display, touch and LVGL are on. LVGL is served in the background, lv.timer_handler() every PERIOD_MS, so the application needs no main loop. Importing again is safe. CONTRACT 1, the version of this contract. A program can test hasattr(display_driver, "CONTRACT") to tell older firmware apart. WIDTH, HEIGHT The logical resolution LVGL draws at. On the RP2350 without PSRAM it is 240x240, shown as 2x2 pixels; with PSRAM 480x480. BUFFERS How many framebuffers the driver uses: 2, or 1 when there was no room for two. PERIOD_MS The period of the background service. indev The touch input device, or None if no touch controller answered. start() Resumes the background service. Calling it while LVGL is being served does nothing. stop() Suspends the background service, and the screen keeps the last image. Calling it twice does nothing. For programs that want their own loop. running() True while LVGL is served in the background, including the short pause after a Ctrl-C (see below). backlight(percent=None) Sets the backlight, from 0 to 100. With no argument it returns the current level. On the STM32H743 boards the backlight is a GPIO for now, so any value above 0 is full brightness; on the STM32F769I-DISCO it is the panel's own brightness (DCS command 0x51).

docs.title: Ctrl-C
docs.text: A Ctrl-C reaches the program, and the screen goes on. That is true whether the program is in a Python loop, for example while True: time.sleep_ms(10), or waits in sys.stdin.read(), as the shell in examples/shell does. The driver is not stopped and does not need start() afterwards.

docs.title: Why the driver has to do something
docs.text:
lv.timer_handler() takes most of the CPU, so a Ctrl-C usually arrives while it runs. It arrives in C, inside a callback that MicroPython's scheduler runs. MicroPython raises a pending Ctrl-C only at a jump in the bytecode. On the ports with threads (ESP32, RP2350) it is raised in whatever Python code runs next. Without help from the driver, that is right after the driver's own try, where the scheduler prints the exception and drops it.

The v0.1.6 drivers did catch the exception, but in the wrong place, so their "stopped by Ctrl-C" path never ran. What happened instead (60 attempts each case, firmware v0.1.6):

Board Program in a Python loop Program in stdin.read() STM32H743 100% reach the program 100% reach the program ESP32-S3 22% (the rest printed and dropped) 25% RP2350 48% 100%

On the STM32H743 MicroPython has no threads. A pending Ctrl-C is never raised inside a scheduled callback there: it waits for the program. So the STM32 drivers already behaved as the contract says, and the code below costs nothing on them.

docs.title: What the driver does
docs.text:
• A jump inside the try of each service callback. This covers _task everywhere, and _tick, the timer callback, on the periodic timers of STM32 and RP2350. A Ctrl-C raised there lands in the driver's except.
  • The KeyboardInterrupt goes back to the program. The driver schedules it again with micropython.schedule(micropython.kbd_intr, None), which is documented MicroPython and needs MICROPY_SCHEDULER_STATIC_NODES, on in all three ports.
  • Then a pause of HOLD_MS (30 ms). Any service run scheduled right behind would get the exception again, so the driver waits before serving LVGL again:
  • on the ESP32, the next one shot run is armed after HOLD_MS;
  • on the periodic timers, the service stops and a one shot timer resumes it. The pause is the cost: the screen stops for about 30 ms on every Ctrl-C. The frame rate is otherwise unchanged (58.3, 42.3 and 28.3 fps, before and after).
  • The touch read callback (gt911.GT911.lv_read_cb) is a Python callback that LVGL calls from inside lv.timer_handler(). It keeps a Ctrl-C that lands in it in touch.interrupted. The driver hands it on after lv.timer_handler() in the same way.

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text:
A Ctrl-C that lands in a Python callback of the application. This means an lv.timer, or an event or animation callback, that LVGL calls from inside lv.timer_handler(). LVGL prints such a Ctrl-C as a traceback and it does not reach the program. It is rare: on the ESP32-S3 it was 2 of 60 attempts, with an lv.timer running a Python loop every 20 ms. It was none of 60 on the RP2350, and it cannot happen on the STM32H743, where a Ctrl-C always waits for the program. An application that needs every Ctrl-C can catch KeyboardInterrupt in its own callbacks.

Measured on the firmware with these drivers frozen in, 2026-11-13, on all three boards: 60 attempts in each of sleep, stdin, cb and sleep with a finger moving on the screen. - STM32H743 (V1.3): every Ctrl-C reached the program once, in all four. 58.3 fps. - RP2350: the same. 28.3 fps. - ESP32-S3: the same, except 2 of 60 in cb, which landed in the application's own lv.timer (see above). 42.3 fps. - The shell in examples/shell stopped sleep 2 and a long cat every time, on all three boards, and vi and edit take Ctrl-C as a key. - The display terminal of the shell, examples/shell/ansiterm.py, needs the same care as the driver. MicroPython calls its write() through os.dupterm, and drops the terminal for good if a KeyboardInterrupt leaves it. On the STM32H743 the serial port is a blocking UART, so a Ctrl-C usually arrives while the same text is being sent, in C, and is raised at the first jump in write(). That jump was before the try: half the Ctrl-C during a long cat were lost there, and the display stopped showing the output. Now the whole of write() is inside the try (docs/log/shell-ctrlc-V13-contract-output*.txt, before and after). - Logs: docs/log/ctrlc-contract-*, docs/log/shell-ctrlc-*-contract.txt, docs/log/editor-ctrlc-4848S040-contract.txt; the measurements before the change, with candidate callbacks in RAM on firmware v0.1.6, are in docs/log/ctrlc-probe-*. - The test: tests/hil/t10_ctrlc_probe.py, run by tests/hil/ctrlc_probe_host.py. - Modes: --mode sleep|stdin|cb. - --expect contract fails unless every Ctrl-C reached the program once and the service never stopped.

docs.title: Deprecated names
docs.text: _task and _timer on every board, and _arm() on the ESP32, were used by examples/shell/ansiterm.py before contract 1: - they stay for this version, so programs written for v0.1.6 keep working; - they go away with contract 2; - a program that replaces display_driver._task still works, but then it also takes over the Ctrl-C handling described above.

docs.title: ESP32-4848S040: notes and measurements
docs.text: ESP32-S3 (240 MHz), 16 MB QIO flash, 8 MB octal PSRAM, 4" 480x480 ST7701 panel on a 16-bit RGB bus, GT911 touch, CH340 on UART0. MicroPython 1.29, LVGL 9.5. This is the first board of the repo on omnipython-lvgl, the successor of the archived lvgl-micropython (the STM32 and RP2350 boards followed on 2026-11-10).

docs.title: Build and bench
docs.text:
• scripts/build.sh esp32 ESP32_4848S040, which hands over to scripts/build_esp32.sh: pins MicroPython, omnipython-lvgl (official, not a fork) and ESP-IDF v5.5.2. MicroPython 1.29 supports the 5.x series only, not ESP-IDF 6.
  • Flash, at offset 0 (the image is complete): esptool.py --chip esp32s3 -p /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 460800 write_flash 0x0 dist/<file>.bin. On a board that had other firmware run esptool.py --chip esp32s3 -p /dev/ttyUSB0 erase_flash first, which erases everything: without it the board can stop at boot with "The filesystem appears to be corrupted".
  • Run tests through the CH340: scripts/uart_run.py <test> --dtr 0 --boot-wait 5. DTR high would hold IO0 low. No native USB (see below).
  • After changing sdkconfig.board or manifest.py, delete .work/esp32/micropython/ports/esp32/build-ESP32_4848S040: an existing build keeps its old sdkconfig, and a failed build its old frozen_content.c, with no warning.
  • A global pip index that does not answer makes every ESP-IDF pip install crawl: the script sets PIP_CONFIG_FILE=/dev/null unless told otherwise.

docs.title: What this board hides
docs.text:
• Native USB must be off. The USB PHY holds GPIO 19 (touch SDA) and 20 (panel G1). MicroPython turns it on by default on the S3, and the only symptom is an empty I2C scan: the bus has its pull-ups, SCL works, SDA cannot go low. MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_USBDEV=0.
  • Red and blue are swapped against the published pin lists: GPIO 4, 5, 6, 7, 15 are the high bits of the pixel, not the low ones. Checked by eye with colour bars and ramps.
  • The panel has no reset line: it keeps its state across a reset of the ESP32, so a change to its init does not show until the next power cycle unless the sequence starts with a software reset (0x01). It does now.
  • Not inverted. The source of the init sequence sends 0x21; here that shows the negative, so the sequence ends with 0x20.
  • GT911 RST and INT are not wired; gt911.GT911(rst=None). Coordinates are panel pixels, no rotation or mirroring (5 targets hit, 1-18 px off = finger size). read() 227 us. The page we took the pins from says SCL is 20 in the text, 45 in its JSON: it is 45.

docs.title: Display driver (modules/esp_rgb)
docs.text:
Same interface as st_ltdc and rgbpanel, on ESP-IDF's esp_lcd. Two framebuffers in PSRAM, outside the GC heap, so the image survives a soft reset. Two bounce buffers of 20 lines in internal RAM, filled by the CPU in an interrupt: the LCD DMA reading PSRAM directly loses pixels when anything else uses that memory. That interrupt copies 24 MB/s and stays on the core that creates the panel, so esp_rgb.init() creates it from a task on the other core: MicroPython keeps its core (loop speed 137 000 -> 145 000/s of 147 000). CONFIG_LCD_RGB_ISR_IRAM_SAFE and CONFIG_SPIRAM_XIP_FROM_PSRAM keep the panel running during flash writes: code and constants run from PSRAM (which is why the heap is 5.7 MB, not 8).

esp_lcd does not report FIFO underruns, so unlike the other drivers there is no counter: lost pixels only show on the panel.

Drive strength of the data lines. At ESP-IDF's default drive (2, about 20 mA) the panel showed coloured specks wherever many bits change from one pixel to the next: single-pixel lines at a quarter, a half and three quarters of a grey ramp, red and green sparkles along the edges of photos. With the data lines at drive 1 (about 10 mA) or 0 the ramp and the photos are clean; the pixel clock at 10 MHz instead of 12, or data on the other clock edge, changed nothing. esp_rgb.init() sets the 16 data lines to MICROPY_HW_RGB_DATA_DRIVE, drive 1 unless the board says otherwise; the pixel clock keeps the default. Checked by eye on one board (dcb4d90487c0), with a grey ramp, the primaries and photos, 21 November 2026.

Soft reset: this port has no board hook after a soft reset, where the other drivers call mp_lv_deinit_gc(), and a later lv.init() panics (LoadProhibited). The board's _boot.py calls esp_rgb.lvgl_guard(), which leaves an object whose finaliser does it, run by gc_sweep_all(). So no patch to MicroPython. Because a board can freeze only one _boot.py, manifest.py lists the port's modules one by one.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Panel 42.20 fps (nominal 42.27 at 12 MHz), the same during 200 KB of flash writes Full refresh, 48 buttons 88 ms after a pause, 94-97 ms back to back Small label change 2.9 ms after a pause gc.collect() with 2 MB of data 120 ms Soft resets with LVGL left initialised 3/3 WiFi see below

Soak of 15 minutes (tests/hil/esp32/t05_soak.py: a full-height bar, a spinner, a label, Python allocations, 2 MB of application data, gc.collect() every 10 s): LVGL 39.1 refreshes/s, panel 42.28 fps, 0 errors, 0 touch errors, memory flat (2.55-2.57 MB free). Log: docs/log/esp32-phase5-soak-4848S040.txt. gc.collect() still stops the animation for 120 ms, about 5 frames.

Where the speed came from. Full refresh, step by step:

panel interrupt on the same core, 16 KB/32 KB caches 145 ms interrupt on the other core 133 ms instruction cache 32 KB, data cache 64 KB, 64-byte lines 88 ms

Everything LVGL touches is behind the cache: code and constants (XIP from PSRAM), the heap and the framebuffers. The caches cost 16 KB of internal RAM. The firmware was already -O2.

Tried and dropped: PARTIAL mode with render buffers in internal RAM (strips copied to the hidden framebuffer, then to the other one). Worse with any height: 112-114 ms at 100 lines against 88, 290 ms at 20 before the caches: each strip walks all the objects again, and the copies add up. Rendering into PSRAM was not the limit.

docs.title: LVGL's memory pools
docs.text:
The pools of lv_mem_core_micropython.c keep LVGL's allocations in TLSF pools held in GC blocks, so they do not walk the GC's allocation table. Since omnipython-lvgl#15 they are opt-in on ESP32 as on the other ports; this board turns them on with LVMP_POOL_TLSF in mpconfigboard.h. LVMP_POOLS=none scripts/build_esp32.sh ESP32_4848S040 builds without them, for comparisons (output -nopool). The first pool is 32 KB and each new one doubles, up to 256 KB.

Measured with two builds of one tree (log docs/log/esp32-pools-c34fbee-4848S040.txt), with the layout script of omnipython-lvgl PR #6. The states are a fresh heap, one free block below 2 MB of bytearrays, and many small holes among them:

no pools pools full refresh, median 70.8-70.9 / 471.0 / 448.7-448.9 ms 70.8-70.9 / 70.9 / 70.9 ms full refresh, worst of 20 71.5 / 471.3 / 472.7 ms 71.4-71.8 / 74.9-75.4 / 71.2-71.3 ms 50 labels created and deleted 30.5 / 70.2 / 230.5 ms 29.0-36.2 / 29.4 / 33.0-34.4 ms gc.collect() 3.1 / 127.1 / 109.9 ms 6.8 / 123.2 / 111.3-111.4 ms GC heap free after display_driver 4.63 MB 4.61 MB

On a heap that has been in use, the pools keep the refresh at its fresh-heap time instead of 6-7x slower. They cost 25 KB of heap and 3.7 ms more per collection on a fresh heap; the 15 minute soak (no holes) runs at 48.9 LVGL refreshes/s with them and 47.6 without. Audio, WiFi and the soak pass with both, 0 errors, memory flat.

Before #15 (v9.5.53, one 256 KB pool, on multi_heap or TLSF: log docs/log/esp32-pools-4848S040.txt) the refresh was the same, but the pools cost 250 KB of heap and 13 ms per collection, and the soak ran at 43.3 refreshes/s against 47.7. From v9.5.53 to c34fbee the firmware grew by 55 KB (the LVGL assert handler of #13 kept file and function names). With CONFIG_SPIRAM_XIP_FROM_PSRAM code and constants are copied to PSRAM, each rounded up to 64 KB pages that the heap does not get: here the constants went from 10 to 11 pages, so the PSRAM region lost 64 KB (the 128 KB written here before was the free GC heap on the other board). omnipython-lvgl 665dec5 (#19: the handler gets only the file's base name and the line) is 50 KB smaller than c34fbee and back to 10 pages: the region is the v9.5.53 size again and gc.mem_free() is 64 KB higher (log docs/log/esp32-psram-665dec5.txt).

docs.title: WiFi
docs.text:
network and socket work as shipped. tests/hil/esp32/t06_wifi.py, with LVGL animating (RSSI read once, after connecting; it moved between -47 and -82 with nothing touched):

Connect 3.9-5.3 s; reconnect 3.9 s HTTP request to the internet, DNS included 91-211 ms Connected, no traffic LVGL 39-46 refreshes/s, longest gap 36-59 ms Largest internal RAM block 128 KB before, 80-88 KB after, not given back by active(False) Panel 42.2-42.3 fps in every phase

TCP download for 10 s, the board reading 4 KB at a time. The first table is the periodic timer of v0.1.2, the second the one-shot timer (see below), 18 downloads in three runs, alternating:

RSSI LVGL Longest gap Speed -48 45.0/s 163 ms 6.07 Mbit/s -82 29.8/s 908 ms 3.66 Mbit/s -45 21.6/s 1015 ms 2.72 Mbit/s -67 11.0/s 912 ms 0.95 Mbit/s Read LVGL Longest gap Speed blocking, settimeout(5) 12.8-47.7/s 113-215 ms 0.35-5.2 Mbit/s non-blocking, sleep_ms(1) when empty 50.5-54.1/s 106-206 ms 0.36-5.7 Mbit/s

Read sockets non-blocking in an application with a UI: a blocking read can wait up to 100 ms in lwip_recvfrom (SOCKET_POLL_US in modsocket.c) without running the scheduler. The gaps of 100-200 ms that remain are not explained, and neither is the speed, which changes from one download to the next with the same reading mode. HTTPS not tried.

docs.title: The schedule queue
docs.text:
MicroPython's schedule queue has 8 places, and a time.sleep_ms() drains it slowly: with a periodic 5 ms timer that schedules a second callback, as display_driver had, a 2 s sleep ran 205 ticks instead of 400. The queue stays full, and whatever else asks for a place is dropped with no error. That was the cause of two problems:

  • the I2S callback of audio.py was lost, and the sound never ended (20 sounds in 24 during long sleeps, none with polling or with the timer stopped);
  • LVGL ran below its rate while sleeping, and the gaps during downloads reached 1 s.

display_driver now uses a one-shot timer, armed again at the end of each lv.timer_handler(), so it holds at most one place. 0 lost callbacks in 72 sounds; t05_perf.py animation from 47 to 55 refreshes/s; soak of 15 minutes 47.6 refreshes/s against 39.1, 42.28 fps, 0 errors, 0 touch errors, memory flat (docs/log/esp32-soak-oneshot-timer-4848S040.txt).

Note: repr() of a machine.Timer on the ESP32 prints the two modes swapped.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
Speaker connector, through an NS4168 on I2S: BCLK GPIO 1, LRCLK GPIO 2, DIN GPIO 40 (pins from a schematic extract on the Home Assistant community, confirmed by ear). These are also the relay pins: audio.py and buzzer.py must not be used on a board with the relays fitted.

audio.py plays beeps, tones and WAV files (PCM, 16 bit, mono or stereo) in the background; buzzer.py goes through it, so the games have sound with no changes. With the bar animating, calls return in 2-12 ms and LVGL keeps its rate, longest gap 25 ms.

  • A sound comes out about 150 ms after the call, the time to cross the buffers.
  • The I2S must keep running until the buffers have played. With one block of silence after the sound, a 60 ms beep was never heard; with two, it is.
  • The amplifier plays one channel: a stereo file loses the other one.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
All 10 examples start without exceptions; Breakout played by hand. Again on omnipython-lvgl c34fbee with the pools (docs/log/esp32-examples-c34fbee-4848S040.txt). On 665dec5 (2026-11-11, second board, docs/log/opl-665dec5-all-boards.txt): panel 42.20 fps, full refresh 93.7 ms on average, LVGL 54.2 refreshes/s animating, and display.set_tile_cnt(256) raises RuntimeError: LVGL assert failed at lv_display.c:614 with LVGL still running. Backlight: PWM on GPIO 38 at 2 kHz, 70% at start, dims at every step down to 10% by eye; display_driver.backlight() drives it from Python, so esp_rgb.backlight() is not the one to use. Below about 30% the panel can no longer be read.

SD card: machine.SDCard(slot=2, sck=48, miso=41, mosi=47, cs=42, freq=10_000_000), after import display_driver: SCK and MOSI are shared with the panel's SPI, which only the start uses. Saving the settings of examples/weather.py tested by hand on a board with a card; no card on the bench board.

Not done: the relays (GPIO 40, 2, 1).

docs.title: Installing the firmware with DFU (STM32 boards)
docs.text:
DFU uses the bootloader in the STM32's ROM over the board's own USB port: no adapter, no wiring, and the board cannot be bricked by a failed attempt, because that bootloader cannot be erased.

Tested on STM32H7_CORE V1.0 with dfu-util 0.11 on Linux. The other STM32 boards have the same ROM bootloader, but this procedure has not been run on them. For a board wired for the UART bootloader see docs/stm32h743.md (Bench).

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• dfu-util: sudo apt install dfu-util on Debian and Ubuntu.
  • A USB data cable, on the board's USB port for the MCU. Some boards have a second port for a USB-serial chip: that one does not do DFU.
  • The firmware as a .dfu file, built with scripts/build.sh:
scripts/build.sh stm32 STM32H7_CORE V10    # dist/STM32H7_CORE-V10-<commit>.dfu

docs.title: 1. Put the board in DFU mode
docs.text:
From a running firmware of this repo built since 2026-11-10, no buttons: in the REPL,

>>> import machine; machine.bootloader()

or mpremote bootloader. The board resets into the ROM bootloader and its serial port goes away. Tested on the STM32H7_CORE V1.0: twice in a row, one with a full write from that DFU. An older firmware resets into MicroPython instead: it jumped to 0x1ff00000, which reads as zeros on the H743, not to the bootloader at 0x1ff09800 (boards/stm32/h743_bootloader.c).

With the buttons, on any firmware or none:

  1. Hold BOOT0.
  2. Press and release RESET, or plug in the USB cable.
  3. Release BOOT0.

The screen stays dark and the board looks dead: that is normal. Check that the computer sees it:

lsusb | grep 0483:df11
# ... ID 0483:df11 STMicroelectronics STM Device in DFU Mode

dfu-util -l
# Found DFU: [0483:df11] ... alt=0, name="@Internal Flash   /0x08000000/16*128Kg" ...

If 0483:df11 does not appear, repeat the steps: BOOT0 must be held at the moment of the reset. Then try another cable.

docs.title: 2. Write the firmware
docs.text:
dfu-util -a 0 -d 0483:df11 -D STM32H7_CORE-V10-<commit>.dfu

It shows a progress bar and ends with:

Download done.
Done parsing DfuSe file

docs.title: 3. Start the firmware
docs.text:
The board stays in DFU mode after writing. Press RESET, without BOOT0, or leave DFU from the computer:

dfu-util -a 0 -d 0483:df11 -s 0x08000000:4:leave -U /tmp/leave.bin   # a file that does not exist yet

It ends with Error during download get_status: normal, the board has already left. With an existing file dfu-util -U refuses to start and the board stays in DFU.

docs.title: 4. Check it
docs.text:
The board comes back as MicroPython, with a serial port and a USB disk:

lsusb | grep f055:9800
# ... ID f055:9800 MicroPython STM32H7 Virtual Comm Port in FS Mode

Open the REPL with any serial terminal, on /dev/ttyACM0 on Linux:

picocom /dev/ttyACM0        # Ctrl-A Ctrl-X to leave

>>> import os, gc
>>> os.uname().machine, gc.mem_free()
('STM32H7_CORE V1.0 with STM32H743', 28670000)
>>> import display_driver      # the panel and the touch start

docs.title: What is kept
docs.text: Only the internal flash is written. The filesystem on the QSPI flash, /flash, the disk that appears on the computer, keeps its files. On a blank QSPI flash MicroPython creates the filesystem at the first start: if your computer offers to format the disk, refuse.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Symptom Cause Cannot open DFU device 0483:df11 or LIBUSB_ERROR_ACCESS No permission on the USB device: on Linux, the dfu-util package installs a udev rule; add your user to plugdev, log in again, or run it with sudo. dfu-util: No DFU capable USB device available Not in DFU mode: repeat step 1. lsusb shows 0483:df11 after step 3 BOOT0 was still held, or RESET was not pressed. Nothing after step 3, no f055:9800 The firmware is for another board or variant: back to step 1, with the right file. Check that the .dfu file matches the board revision.

docs.title: Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-4: performance and memory
docs.text: Measured on the board (RP2350B, 16 MB flash, no PSRAM: U9 not fitted), MicroPython v1.29.0, MICROPY_HW_RGBPANEL_SCALE = 2 (240x240 framebuffer shown as 2x2 pixels). LVGL 9.5 through PyDevices omnipython-lvgl (c34fbee since 2026-11-10, 665dec5 since 2026-11-11: the same numbers, 46 KB less flash, see the end of the next section) with its memory pools (next section); the sections after it were measured before, on lvgl-micropython 3e287e7 / lvgl-bindings 7740c2f, the same LVGL. Raw logs in docs/log/.

docs.title: omnipython-lvgl and LVGL's memory pools (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
The board moved from the archived lvgl-micropython to omnipython-lvgl c34fbee, like the other boards, with LVGL's memory pools on (LVMP_POOL_TLSF in mpconfigboard.h; the binding's TLSF pools, held in GC blocks, from 32 KB doubling up to 256 KB). Measured on board 2, whose GT911 does not answer (log/board2-check.txt), so without touch, log/rp2350-opl-c34fbee.txt:

  • Same image: the 64 tile CRCs of t04_crc.py match the earlier ones (and the unix port).
  • Same speed on a clean heap: t06_perf.py 16.6 ms at 150 MHz, 13.1 ms at 200 and 240 MHz (two buffers, so frame-bound), 57.67 / 76.67 fps, no underruns.
  • t02_lvgl_smoke.py across soft resets, t03_panel.py (57.80 fps, 0 underruns, flash writes included), t07_lvgl_oom.py as before (the half-done refresh after a MemoryError is still there, docs/upstream/pydevices-issue-oom-render.md).
  • 26 KB less free heap: 190 KB after import display_driver instead of 215 KB.
  • 1 h soak (t06_soak.py, two buffers): 57.73 fps, 0 underruns, 0 errors, lowest free heap 151 KB (84 KB before), 668 800 Python allocations (374 400 before, in the same hour) (log/rp2350-soak-opl.txt).
  • The 10 examples start and keep running, 151-189 KB free, 0 underruns; not played, no touch on this board (log/rp2350-examples-opl.txt).
  • Board 1 (with touch), the same file: the same figures (CRCs, perf, heap states), LVGL clicks 3/3, the 5 touch targets at the corners and centre, GT911 read() 200 us (236 before), the 10 examples start, Breakout played by hand: touch responsive, no glitches (log/rp2350-board1-opl.txt).

The pools fix the open issue below. lv.refr_now() of scene_static after a 60 ms pause, median of 15, the same firmware built with and without the pools (LVMP_POOLS=none), log/rp2350-heap-states-opl.txt:

heap two buffers, no pools two buffers, pools one buffer, no pools one buffer, pools clean 26.5 ms 26.5 ms 10.5 ms 9.6 ms 30 KB of garbage 26.0 ms 26.5 ms 9.3 ms 9.6 ms 60 KB of small live objects 43.2 ms 26.5 ms 9.3 ms 9.6 ms small live objects with holes 43.8 ms 26.5 ms 17.0 ms 9.6 ms

With the pools every heap state costs the same. Without them the extra time appears in the same kind of heap states as in the table of 2026-11-05 below: so it was LVGL's allocations walking the GC heap (gc_alloc() starts from the first free block), as on the STM32H7_CORE (docs/stm32h743.md). The two-buffer figures include the wait for the end of the frame.

The pool layout script of the STM32 boards (24 buttons and 6 sliders, a 2 KB block per hole, 80 KB, log/rp2350-pool-layouts-opl.txt) shows the same with two buffers (refresh 51.8 ms in every layout with the pools, 34.5 ms fresh and 68.9 ms fragmented without); with one buffer its scene renders in 35.2 ms with the pools, 33.6-33.9 ms without, so here the pools cost 1.6 ms when the heap is not in the way. gc.collect(): 2.3-5.2 ms with the pools, 2.0-5.0 ms without.

omnipython-lvgl 665dec5 (2026-11-11, board 1, log/opl-665dec5-all-boards.txt): its PR #19 makes an LVGL assert pass only the file's base name and the line, 46,336 B less flash. Same 64 tile CRCs, the same t06_perf.py figures (57.67 / 76.67 fps, 13.1 ms at 200 MHz), the same 350 KB free after boot, and display.set_tile_cnt(256) raises RuntimeError: LVGL assert failed at lv_display.c:614 with LVGL still running.

docs.title: Scan-out and rendering vs clock
docs.text:
Core voltage untouched (default 1.10 V). machine.freq() then rgbpanel.init(pclk_hz=...). refr_now = full-screen invalidated lv.refr_now() of tests/hil/scene_static.py, single buffer (no wait for the buffer swap). Source: log/phase6-perf.txt.

sys clock PCLK divider fps measured (nominal) refr_now avg underruns (3 s / 200 KB flash write) 150 MHz 15 MHz 5 57.67 (57.73) 9.23 ms 0 / 0 200 MHz 20 MHz 5 76.67 (76.97) 7.86 ms 0 / 0 240 MHz 20 MHz 6 76.67 (76.97) 7.25 ms 0 / 0

Rendering speeds up less than the clock (150 → 240 MHz = x1.6, refr_now x1.27): code runs from QSPI flash (XIP), whose clock divider MicroPython raises with the system clock.

Long flash-write test at 150 MHz: 107 x 200 KB in 90 s, 5219 frames (57.73 fps), 0 underruns, no visible glitch (log/phase3-flash-stress.txt).

docs.title: Tearing and double buffering
docs.text:
With one framebuffer LVGL (DIRECT mode) draws into the buffer being scanned out: a vertical bar sweeping across the screen showed visibly broken/offset (Nunzio, by eye). Waiting for VSYNC in the flush callback cannot help in that mode (the drawing is already done when flush is called).

Fix: double buffering at 240x240, which fits in SRAM (a second 480x480 buffer would not). rgbpanel.init(buffers=2) allocates a second framebuffer and its list of control blocks on the GC heap (122 896 B). The DMA block that ends every frame reads the list for the next frame from a variable: pointing it at the other list swaps buffers exactly at the end of a frame, in hardware, with no ISR. swap() returns once the control DMA channel reads from the new list (so the old buffer is no longer read). LVGL draws into the hidden buffer; the flush callback (in C) swaps. Result: bar straight, movement smooth (by eye).

display_driver uses two buffers by default (falls back to one on MemoryError). Full-screen lv.refr_now() then takes ~17 ms (9.2 ms rendering + wait for the end of the frame): LVGL refreshes at most once per panel frame (57.7 Hz at PCLK 15 MHz). Pixel check vs the unix port still 64/64 tiles identical (log/phase6-crc-doublebuf.txt).

docs.title: Was open: a full redraw sometimes costs one frame more with two buffers
docs.text:
Solved by LVGL's memory pools: see above. The analysis as it was on 2026-11-05:

tests/hil/t06_perf.py no longer reproduces the table above: display_driver now uses two buffers, so refr_now includes the wait for the swap and reads the frame, not the rendering (17.2 ms at 57.7 Hz, 12.9 ms at 77 Hz). Back to back, or from a pause that ends early enough, it can read two frames (26 and 34 ms). This is no regression: the published firmware and the omnipython-lvgl build give the same figures.

Measured on the 240x240 scene (2026-11-05, 150 MHz), lv.refr_now() after a pause:

heap one buffer two buffers clean 9.5 ms 11.5 ms 30 KB of garbage 8.9 ms 28.8 ms 60 KB of small live objects 8.9 ms 28.8 ms small live objects with holes 14.7 ms 28.8 ms

Timed inside the flush: the wait for the swap stays short (3 ms); LVGL reaches the flush at 9.4 ms in the first case and 24.7 ms in the slow one. So the extra 15 ms are in LVGL, before the flush, and only with two buffers.

Ruled out, by measurement: free memory (slow with over 200 KB free), gc.collect() as a remedy, the flash clock (QMI M0_TIMING unchanged), the XIP cache (same misses), flash writes as such, one extra refresh (one REFR_START per refr_now), and the second framebuffer being in the GC heap (a static one gives the same figures, and loses 120 KB with one buffer).

Not known: where the 15 ms go, and why they depend on the heap. They look like a copy of the 115 KB between the buffers, but refr_sync_areas() should have nothing to copy with the whole screen invalidated. Python event callbacks on the display made the slowdown disappear for the same garbage, probably by changing the heap, so timing from Python does not settle it: the next step is timing inside LVGL, in C, with nothing that allocates.

Effect: full-screen redraws at about 34 per second instead of 57 in those heap states; the image stays correct. Small redraws were not measured in those states.

docs.title: Robustness: Ctrl-C and soft reset
docs.text:
• Flush callback in C (rgbpanel.lv_display_create()): with a Python flush_cb, a KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl-C, or the Ctrl-C mpremote sends before every command) landing inside it is printed and swallowed by the binding, flush_ready() is never called, and LVGL's next refresh waits for the flush forever: the board hung (USB up, REPL dead, power cycle needed). With the Python flush + double buffer the board hung in 2 of 3 soft-reset sequences (the third passed by timing luck); with the C flush 6/6 soft resets with LVGL live were clean (log/phase6-softreset-debug.txt).
  • Ctrl-C reaches the program: lv.timer_handler() takes most of the CPU, so a KeyboardInterrupt usually lands in display_driver's callbacks; there it now stops the timer, and the next Ctrl-C reaches the program (mpremote sends several). 3/3 interrupts of a running LVGL program succeeded at the first mpremote attempt (log/phase6-ctrlc.txt). display_driver.start() resumes.
  • Soft reset: the board hook moves the image to the static framebuffer if the GC one was shown, drops the GC buffer, and clears LVGL's root (binding bug, see upstream/pydevices-issue-soft-reset.md). Scan-out keeps running throughout.

docs.title: Soak tests (150 MHz)
docs.text:
Configuration Duration Frames fps Underruns Errors Python allocations GC free, per-minute samples (t ≥ 60 s) single buffer, Python flush 3600 s 207 823 57.73 0 0 668 760 252 848 .. 270 912 B double buffer, C flush 3600 s 207 828 57.73 0 0 374 400 66 688 .. 147 952 B

Scene: sweeping bar animation, spinner, label updated 5x/s, list/string churn, gc.collect() every 10 s (tests/hil/t06_soak.py, log/phase6-soak.txt, log/phase6-soak-doublebuf.txt).

  • No leak: GC free has no trend over the hour in either run. The samples are taken between collections, so they include garbage; the single 66 688 B sample in the double buffer run is one such instant (the next minute is back at 139 840 B).
  • The min_free column printed by the test is not meaningful: its starting value is gc.mem_free() before the first gc.collect() and no later sample went below it.
  • The Python loop ran ~44 % fewer iterations with double buffering (allocation count): most likely because the flush busy-waits for the end of the panel frame on every refresh, which leaves less CPU to the main loop at 150 MHz.

docs.title: Changing machine.freq()
docs.text: The scan-out runs from clk_sys: after machine.freq(f) the PCLK scales with it until rgbpanel.init(pclk_hz=...) is called. init() notices the new system clock and restarts the scan-out with the new divider (panel not re-initialised, framebuffer kept, the shown buffer kept). Only integer dividers are accepted: e.g. 200 MHz with 15 MHz PCLK is refused with ValueError (no fractional-divider jitter). Decision: the driver does not follow clock changes by itself (MicroPython has no hook for that); applications call rgbpanel.init() after machine.freq(). The GT911 (I2C1, 400 kHz) answers normally at 240 MHz and back at 150 MHz without re-initialisation (log/phase6-touch-freq.txt).

docs.title: SRAM map (520 KiB, firmware with LVGL + rgbpanel + display_driver)
docs.text:
From firmware.elf (arm-none-eabi-size -A, nm):

Region Bytes Notes vector table + .data 18 808 includes code copied to RAM .bss total 135 900 — rgbpanel_fb (240x240 RGB565) 115 200 static, scanned out by DMA — rgbpanel_cb (481 control blocks) 7 696 — mp_state_ctx 9 076 — rest 3 928 C heap (.heap) 2 048 MicroPython GC heap 365 476 __GcHeapStart 0x20025c5c .. __GcHeapEnd 0x2007f000 core 1 stack 4 096 0x2007f000 .. 0x20080000 core 0 stack (SCRATCH_X/Y) 8 192 0x20080000 .. 0x20082000

GC heap free (gc.mem_free()): 345 056 B with rgbpanel only; 331 968 B right after import display_driver; ~274 000 B with a small LVGL scene and touch.

With a second framebuffer for double buffering (init(buffers=2), GC heap): 115 200 + 7 696 B more: gc.mem_free() ~211 000 B right after import display_driver with two buffers and touch.

480x480 is not possible without PSRAM: a 460 800 B framebuffer leaves ~27 KiB of SRAM heap for everything else. With PSRAM the GC heap moves to PSRAM and the framebuffer takes the SRAM heap area instead (next section).

docs.title: PSRAM (2026-11-20)
docs.text:
Board 1 with an 8 MB PSRAM (APS6404L) fitted on U9 by the owner. Full log: log/rp2350-psram-probe-2026-11-20.txt, soak log/rp2350-psram480-soak-2026-11-20.txt.

The memory. Detected at boot on CS GPIO47 by v0.1.7 as is: GC heap 8 553 280 B. 8 patterns over 8 192 000 B, 0 errors, at the QMI's 75 MHz (150 MHz system clock) and at 120 MHz (240 MHz). The Ctrl-C contract (4 x 60) passed with the heap in PSRAM, 28.3 fps as before.

Bandwidth. DMA read of one 480x480 frame: 26.7 / 28.1 MB/s (cached / uncached alias) at 150 MHz, 42.8 / 45.6 MB/s at 240 MHz, the same with the CPU reading or writing PSRAM. A 480x480 scan-out needs 26.6 MB/s on average, 30 MB/s within a line at PCLK 15 MHz.

Why the framebuffer cannot be in PSRAM. Bandwidth is not the problem; the PIO FIFO holds 16 pixels (1.1 us at 15 MHz) and any DMA access to XIP holds the DMA engine up for 2-4 us, also for channels that only read SRAM. Measured on v0.1.7 (240x240 from SRAM), underruns in 20 s while a second DMA channel copies in a loop:

Second channel Underruns none 0 PSRAM to SRAM 401 (every poll) SRAM to SRAM 0 XIP stream FIFO (PSRAM, paced by DREQ_XIP_STREAM) 399

With the PSRAM copy running, the scan-out is clean from PCLK 7.5 MHz on (x2: the FIFO covers 4.3 us), not at 15 MHz (2.1 us); a 480x480 scan-out would need ~3.75 MHz (14 Hz). The CPU reading PSRAM does not disturb the DMA (0 underruns).

Tried and dropped: - Framebuffer in PSRAM, read by the panel DMA: the PIO stalls and stays late (the line-start IRQ is already pending), the picture shifts right with stray pixels. - An 8-line ring in SRAM filled by two more DMA channels from PSRAM: the same stalls, through the shared DMA engine. - Core 1 copying lines into the ring: clean when idle (38.5 Hz at PCLK 10 MHz; one core copies ~20 MB/s at 240 MHz), but core 0 writing PSRAM (LVGL drawing) starves it: 94 % of the lines late, i.e. shown 8 lines off.

What the firmware does (modules/rgbpanel, patches/micropython): at boot, before gc_init(), the board hook MICROPY_BOARD_SRAM_HEAP takes the framebuffer from the end of the SRAM heap area: 480x480 with PSRAM (the GC heap is then PSRAM only), 240x240 without. With PSRAM the system clock goes to 240 MHz before the flash and PSRAM timing is set. Measured (docs/log/rp2350-psram-probe-2026-11-20.txt): - 57.70 fps at PCLK 15 MHz, 0 underruns, also with core 0 writing or reading 1 MB of PSRAM; - t03_panel.py: 57.80 fps, 0 underruns, 0 during 200 KB of flash writes; - Ctrl-C contract 60/60 in all four cases (sleep, stdin, cb, touch), LVGL 28.7 fps with one buffer (log/ctrlc-contract-RP2350-psram480-*.txt); - touch at 1:1: five targets (corners, centre) all hit; - GC heap 8 215 616 B, 8.2 MB free; - soak (t06_soak.py, one buffer, stopped at 30 min instead of 1 h): 57.74 fps, 0 underruns, 0 errors, 240 640 Python allocations, lowest free heap 8 132 576 B, steady at ~8.14 MB (log/rp2350-psram480-soak-2026-11-20.txt).

One buffer only: a second 480x480 buffer would be on the GC heap in PSRAM, which the panel DMA must not read, so init(buffers=2) raises MemoryError. Applications must also keep rp2.DMA off PSRAM and flash addresses while the panel runs, at either scale.

docs.title: STM32H743 boards: design notes and measurements
docs.text: DEV190806042, FK743M5-XIH6, STM32H7_CORE V1.0 / V1.3 on MicroPython 1.29.0 with the PyDevices LVGL binding (LVGL 9.5): omnipython-lvgl (its ports/micropython) since 2026-11-10, before that the archived lvgl-micropython with a patch in patches/lvgl-micropython/ (removed when the RP2350 board moved too; in the git history). The old port and its sources are described in docs/stm32-inventory.md. Work in progress: filled in phase by phase.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
• Out-of-tree boards in boards/stm32/<BOARD>/ (BOARD_DIR), STM32H7_CORE with BOARD_VARIANT=V10|V13 (required). scripts/build.sh stm32 <BOARD> [VARIANT].
  • Binding: scripts/build.sh clones omnipython-lvgl at a pinned commit (OPL_SHA) into $WORK_DIR/omnipython-lvgl and passes LVMP_DIR=.../ports/micropython; no patches. A build directory made with the other binding fails ("duplicate member lvmp_pool_mem" among the root pointers): delete .work/micropython/ports/stm32/build-<NAME> after a binding switch.
  • manifest.py: LVGL ($(LVMP_DIR)/manifest.py) and modules/st_ltdc; manifest_nolvgl.py: modules/st_ltdc only (bring-up). With FROZEN_MANIFEST=.../manifest_nolvgl.py the build goes to build-<NAME>-nolvgl and dist/<NAME>-nolvgl-*.
  • Floats: Python floats stay double (MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL = double, as in the old port; the H743 FPU is double precision). The port then links only MicroPython's double libm, while LVGL 9.5 calls sinf, cosf, atan2f, sqrtf (lv_arclabel.c, lv_indev_gesture.c): undefined at link time. Fixed on the board side, no patch: boards/stm32/lvgl_libm.mk adds the single-precision files of lib/libm that provide them.
  • Soft reset: MICROPY_BOARD_END_SOFT_RESET = st_ltdc_board_end_soft_reset() (modules/st_ltdc/st_ltdc.c): mp_lv_deinit_gc() when LVGL is built in, then the port's own boardctrl_end_soft_reset(). Test: tests/hil/stm32/t02_lvgl_softreset.py.
  • Size: about 1.12 MB of the 2 MB internal flash, 945–953 KiB free (table in docs/stm32-inventory.md).

docs.title: Display driver (modules/st_ltdc)
docs.text:
API (module st_ltdc, aligned with rgbpanel of the RP2350): init(width, height, hsync, hbp, hfp, vsync, vbp, vfp, *, polarity=0, pclk_hz=50_000_000, buffers=2, backlight=100), deinit(), framebuffer(i=0), shown(), swap(timeout_ms=100), backlight([pct]), frame_count(), underruns(), wait_vsync(timeout_ms=100), info(), and with LVGL lv_display_create(partial_lines=0), lv_tick_install(). Panel timings: python/panels.py (st_ltdc.init(**panels.get("IPS1024x600"))).

Choices:

  • Framebuffers outside the GC heap (option b of the plan): the top MICROPY_HW_LTDC_FB_BYTES = 4 MB of the SDRAM (0xC1C00000-0xC1FFFFFF), the heap ends below it (MICROPY_HEAP_END, 28 MB of heap). Room for two 1024x600 RGB565 buffers (2 x 1 228 800 B) and the PARTIAL render buffers. Never freed: the LTDC keeps scanning valid memory across a soft reset and the image stays (as on the RP2350); no root pointers, nothing to rescue in the soft-reset hook. The old driver used m_malloc on the heap, which a soft reset frees while the LTDC still reads it.
  • Write-through MPU region on exactly that zone, region 15. Not region 6 as in the old driver: since 1.29 dma.c (dma_protect_rx_region, SD card reads) reprograms and then disables regions 6 and 7, which would silently turn the framebuffers back to write-back after the first SD read. The zone is 4 MB aligned, as the MPU needs.
  • Registers programmed directly (LTDC, DMA2D; PLL3 through HAL_RCCEx_PeriphCLKConfig): no HAL LTDC/DMA2D sources, no hal_conf changes, no HAL_LTDC_MspInit per board. Pins are data in each mpconfigboard.h (MICROPY_HW_LTDC_PINS), checked against boards/stm32h743_af.csv and against the other pins of each board.
  • Pixel clock at run time: PLL3 M=5 (5 MHz reference), N and R searched for the closest output, VCO 192-836 MHz. 50 MHz gives N=40, R=4, the old fixed setting.
  • Swap without an ISR doing LVGL work: the flush writes the new layer address and asks for a reload at vertical blanking, and returns with the flush pending; LVGL's flush_wait_cb polls until the LTDC has taken it (at most one frame), which LVGL calls only before it touches the buffer that was on screen, at the start of the next refresh. Phase 5: before, the flush itself waited (up to 17 ms per refresh). The only interrupt handler counts frames (line interrupt after the active area), FIFO underruns and transfer errors. On the H7 these are two vectors: LTDC_IRQn (line) and LTDC_ER_IRQn (underrun, transfer error); the first build enabled only the first, so underruns could not be counted (found on hardware, fixed). Priority 5, above IRQ_PRI_FLASH (6): spibdev.c raises BASEPRI to it for a whole QSPI erase/program, and at IRQ_PRI_TIMX (13) the frame counter dropped to 19 fps during writes (docs/log/stm32-phase3-flash-stress-V13-before-fix.txt); now 58.3.
  • PARTIAL mode: render buffers in the zone (write-through, so the DMA2D reads what the CPU wrote), each area copied by the DMA2D into the shown buffer, synchronously.
  • AXI QoS as in the old driver (SDRAM target 1 outstanding transaction, LTDC and DMA2D before the CPU). Measured in phase 5: no effect either way (CPU benchmarks, LVGL refresh times and underruns are the same with the registers at reset values); kept as it was.
  • Backlight: GPIO on/off (MICROPY_HW_LTDC_BL, active high as in the old driver, MICROPY_HW_LTDC_BL_ACTIVE); PWM after the polarity is confirmed by eye.
  • RGB565 only (LVGL's colour depth in the PyDevices lv_conf.h is 16).

Tests: tests/hil/stm32/t03_panel.py (patterns A-D, frame rate, underruns, flash write), tests/hil/stm32/flash_stress.py, tests/hil/stm32/t03_softreset.py. The Python side of the first two was run on the unix port with a stand-in st_ltdc (pattern pixels checked: corners, bar colours, 32/64 ramp steps), then on hardware (below).

docs.title: Touch and display_driver (phase 4)
docs.text:
• python/stm32_board.py (frozen): touch wiring per board, picked from os.uname().machine; stm32_board.touch() returns a gt911.GT911 (the same python/gt911.py as the RP2350, pins given by name) on SoftI2C or hardware I2C at 400 kHz; stm32_board.panel() reads PANEL from /flash/display_config.py.
  • python/stm32/display_driver.py (frozen as display_driver, LVGL builds only): same interface as the RP2350 one (import display_driver; disp, touch, indev, start(), stop(), WIDTH, HEIGHT): st_ltdc.init() with the panel timings, DIRECT mode on two framebuffers, lv.timer_handler() every 5 ms from a soft Timer(-1).
  • GT911 on the V1.3 (IPS1024x600): fw 0x1060, config v130, 1024x600 in its own config, so coordinates are panel pixels (scale 1); address 0x5D; command register 0xFF after power-on, set to 0 by GT911() as on the RP2350.
  • Measured on the V1.3: orientation, no rotation or mirroring (5 targets hit, 4-15 px off = finger size, docs/log/stm32-phase4-t04_touch_paint-V13.txt); read() with no touch 124 us bare, 229 us with LVGL running; LVGL button 5 taps = 5 clicks, read_cb every ~33 ms (LVGL's indev period), max 446 us, 0 underruns (docs/log/stm32-phase4-t04_click-V13.txt).

docs.title: Performance (phase 5)
docs.text:
Measured on the V1.3 with the IPS1024x600 at 58.3 Hz (tests/hil/stm32/t05_perf.py, logs docs/log/stm32-phase5-*-V13.txt).

  • SDRAM bandwidth is the limit. 16-bit bus at 120 MHz: CPU reads about 150 MB/s with the LTDC off, about 95 MB/s while it scans out (it takes 1024 x 600 x 2 x 58 = 71 MB/s); SDRAM to SDRAM copies 45-65 MB/s (CPU or DMA2D); writes from AXI SRAM to SDRAM 137-145 MB/s. Bank conflicts with the LTDC cost little (90 against ~100 MB/s). The heap's write-back cache is slower for streaming writes than the write-through zone (49 against 142 MB/s: write-allocate reads every line first).
  • CPU cost of the LTDC: Python code +0-1 % (runs from cache); 1 MB copies -34 %, gc.collect() +20-24 %.
  • LVGL allocations were the real bottleneck. The binding allocates LVGL memory with gc_alloc(), which walks the allocation table from the first free block; a multi-block allocation does not move that hint. With 2 MB of bytearrays behind a free block, an 8 KB allocation cost 611 us instead of 181 and a full refresh of 48 buttons 575 ms instead of 54 (the refresh makes about 1200 allocations). Fixed by patches/lvgl-micropython/0001-lvmp-pools-on-lvgl-tlsf.patch (now in the git history): the binding's ESP32 pools (LVGL memory in 256 KB TLSF pools that are GC blocks behind a root pointer, so the GC still sees every object LVGL refers to) extended to other ports with LVGL's own TLSF, enabled for these boards by boards/stm32/lvgl_pool.mk (LVMP_POOL_TLSF=1). Now 50-51 ms in every heap state. Since omnipython-lvgl c34fbee (its PR #15) the pools are the binding's own (lvmp_pool.h, opt-in with LVMP_POOL_TLSF=1 on every port): the first is 32 KB, each new one twice the last up to 256 KB. Checked: 300 callbacks reachable only through LVGL survive garbage and collections, also after lv.deinit()/lv.init() and soft resets (tests/hil/stm32/t05_lvgl_gc.py); memory back to the same value after lv.deinit().
  • LVGL on the panel, scene of 48 buttons, 2 MB of bytearrays in the heap, after the fix:
mode full refresh small label change DIRECT, 2 buffers (display_driver) 56-66 ms 17-18 ms (waits for vertical blanking) DIRECT, 1 buffer 52 ms 0.9-1.2 ms (tearing possible) PARTIAL, 60 lines 86 ms 0.9-1.2 ms PARTIAL, 200 lines 78 ms 0.8-1.2 ms

Before the fix: 273, 257, 384, 243 ms. 0 underruns in every case. - Pools against no pools, same tree (V1.0, 2026-11-10; the layout script of omnipython-lvgl PR #6, log docs/log/stm32-pool-layouts-V10.txt; the build without pools is LVMP_POOLS=none scripts/build.sh stm32 STM32H7_CORE V10). Fresh heap / one free block below 2 MB of bytearrays / many small holes among them:

no pools pools full refresh, median 68.6 / 359.3 / 360.0 ms 68.6 / 68.6 / 68.6 ms full refresh, worst of 20 68.8 / 359.8 / 370.7 ms 68.7 / 68.7 / 68.7 ms 50 labels created and deleted 15.6 / 31.6 / 93.7 ms 14.5 / 14.5 / 17.9 ms gc.collect() 31.7 / 81.0 / 77.1 ms 37.6 / 87.0 / 82.9 ms

The pools cost about 6 ms per collection and 250 KB of heap on a fresh heap, nothing on the refresh.

The same on omnipython-lvgl c34fbee, growing pools (log docs/log/stm32-pool-layouts-opl-V10.txt, 2 runs each, identical within 1 ms):

no pools pools full refresh, median 68.6 / 359.3 / 360.0 ms 68.6 / 68.6 / 68.6 ms full refresh, worst of 20 68.8 / 359.8 / 371.1 ms 68.7 / 68.7 / 68.7 ms 50 labels created and deleted 16.8 / 32.6 / 94.0 ms 15.6 / 15.6 / 19.0 ms gc.collect() 31.8 / 81.0 / 77.2 ms 33.3 / 82.5 / 78.5 ms heap free after import display_driver 28 670 368 B 28 644 816 B

Now the pools cost 25 KB of heap and 1.5 ms per collection. Without pools the binding switch changes nothing.

Small heap: the GC heap in the AXI SRAM, 490 KB (GC_HEAP=axi, STM32H7_CORE only; the framebuffers stay in SDRAM), the same script with 256 KB of bytearrays (PAD = 128), log docs/log/stm32-pool-layouts-axi-V10.txt:

AXI, no pools AXI, pools SDRAM, pools full refresh, median 51.4 / 85.6 / 85.7 ms 51.4 / 51.4 / 51.4 ms 68.6 / 68.6 / 68.6 ms full refresh, worst of 20 61.8 / 85.9 / 93.0 ms 58.2 / 54.8 / 57.3 ms 68.6 / 68.7 / 68.7 ms 50 labels created and deleted 12.3 / 13.5 / 12.1 ms 12.6 / 12.6 / 12.6 ms 15.5 / 15.7 / 15.7 ms gc.collect() 1.4 / 4.9 / 4.8 ms 2.0 / 5.5 / 5.5 ms 33.4 / 40.5 / 39.7 ms heap free after import display_driver 461 968 B 436 224 B 28 644 800 B

One hole is enough to slow the refresh by two thirds without pools, also on a small heap; with them it does not move. Their cost there: 25 KB, about 5 % of the heap, and 0.6 ms per collection. A heap in AXI SRAM also renders faster (51 against 69 ms). - Animation rate (tests/hil/stm32/t05_soak.py: a full-height bar sweeping, a spinner, a label, Python allocations, 2 MB of application data): LVGL refreshes per second 19.2 with the blocking flush and LVGL's 33 ms refresh period, 34.5 with the flush wait moved to flush_wait_cb and display_driver.REFR_PERIOD_MS = 16. Not 58: the 16 ms LVGL timer is not locked to the 17.15 ms frame, and each refresh re-renders the spinner and copies the changed areas between the two SDRAM buffers. No tearing (bar straight, by eye). - GT911 over SoftI2C: 1 OSError (ENODEV) in about 9000 polls (3 in the 15 min soak). gt911.lv_read_cb now keeps the last state and counts it in touch.errors instead of raising out of LVGL's input read. Not explained yet; a suspect is SoftI2C's clock-stretching timeout (255 us by default). Both buses ran above the GT911's 400 kHz (2026-11-10). The port's hardware I2C timings are for a 54 MHz kernel clock and these boards clock I2C from PCLK at 120 MHz: freq=400_000 gave 1.07 MHz on the V1.0's I2C4. SoftI2C rounds its half period to whole microseconds: 400 kHz asked, 500 kHz run. Address NACKs on the V1.0, polling every 2 ms without a touch, one run of 1 min and one of 5 min per setting (docs/log/stm32-gt911-rate-V10.txt):

bus clock errors I2C4, freq=400_000 1.07 MHz 2 in 155 000 reads I2C4, timingr=0x5072121A about 400 kHz 0 in 153 000 I2C4, freq=100_000 278 kHz 0 in 152 000 SoftI2C, freq=400_000 500 kHz 3 in 154 000 (all in the first minute) SoftI2C, freq=200_000 250 kHz 0 in 121 000

All five errors above the rating, none within it: a hint, not a proof (with one rate for all, about a 3 % chance). stm32_board.touch_i2c() now runs the bus within the rating: TOUCH_TIMINGR (400 kHz at 120 MHz) on hardware I2C, 250 kHz on SoftI2C. The error count in touch.errors stays. Checked on the V1.0 with it: 15 min soak with 0 touch errors (2 before), 5/5 taps (t04_click.py); a read with no touch takes 241 us instead of 80. - Possible next step, not done: PARTIAL render buffers in AXI SRAM (unused when the GC heap is in SDRAM). Rendering alone took 33 ms there against 53-59 ms in SDRAM, and the DMA2D copies AXI to SDRAM at 137 MB/s against 48 from SDRAM.

docs.title: Bench: flashing and running tests over UART1 (STM32H7_CORE V1.3)
docs.text:
The V1.3 on the bench is wired to a CH340 USB-serial adapter on UART1 (PA9/PA10, the second REPL) with DTR -> BOOT0 and RTS -> NRST; native USB is not connected. Measured line levels: DTR=0 puts BOOT0 high, RTS=1 holds NRST low.

  • scripts/stm32_uart_flash.py flash <fw>.hex --verify: ST system bootloader over the UART (AN3155, v3.1, chip id 0x450), erases only the sectors in the image. Full LVGL image: 9-10 sectors, about 3 min at 115200 with verify. From sector 8 on (bank 2, images over 1 MB, as v0.1.5 for the V1.3) the bootloader ACKs the erase before bank 2 is done and erases it with nothing on the line: a command sent meanwhile gets no answer, and a reset then left the first sectors of bank 2 half erased (zeros, hanging reads, a failed verify). The script now waits in silence until the bootloader answers again (about 5 s for 2 sectors). All four STM32 .hex files of v0.1.5 reach bank 2: with the script of v0.1.5 or older the flash fails (cmd 31: timeout after the erase); flash again with the fixed script, which erases the image's sectors again (docs/log/stm32-uart-flash-bank2-V13.txt). machine.bootloader() from the old 1.27 firmware did not reach USB DFU (it reset into MicroPython); fixed in this repo on 2026-11-10, see docs/flash-dfu.md.
  • scripts/uart_run.py a.py [b.py ...] [--soft-reset]: raw REPL runner, like mpremote run. Linux raises DTR/RTS for a moment at every open of the port, and that pulse on RTS hard-resets the board; mpremote toggles them too. So every call starts from a fresh boot, and soft-reset tests must run as several scripts in one call. The first runs of t02/t03 soft-reset tests were invalid for this reason (ticks_ms about 2.7 s, reset_cause 2) and were repeated in one session.
  • Over the V1.0's own USB (/dev/ttyACM0) the opposite holds: opening the port resets nothing. A soak run as the only script of a call ran on what the perf test had left (display_driver imported, its display gone): 0 LVGL refreshes counted, 4 MB less heap, and still "RESULT: ok". --soft-reset now resets before the first script too.

docs.title: Build commands
docs.text:
scripts/build_rp2.sh does all of this with the pins above (sources in .work/ unless WORK_DIR is set). By hand, in the workspace:

export PATH=$PWD/tools/xpack-arm-none-eabi-gcc-15.2.1-1.1/bin:$PATH
B=$PWD/copper-and-code-mcu-boards/boards/rp2/WAVESHARE_RP2350_TOUCH_LCD_4

make -C micropython/ports/rp2 BOARD_DIR=$B BUILD=build-TLCD4 -j

MicroPython 1.29 takes the LVGL C module from the manifest (include("$(LVMP_DIR)/manifest.py"), which calls c_module(".")), not from USER_C_MODULES. LVMP_DIR reaches the manifest as the CMake variable MICROPY_MANIFEST_LVMP_DIR, set in mpconfigboard.cmake.

docs.title: Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-4
docs.text:
Upstream MicroPython v1.29 with LVGL 9.5 (import lvgl as lv, PyDevices binding) for the Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-4: RP2350B, 16 MB flash, 4" 480x480 ST7701S RGB panel, GT911 capacitive touch.

This is an out-of-tree board: no fork of MicroPython or of the LVGL binding. The RGB panel is driven by rgbpanel, a user C module in this repo (PIO + DMA, no CPU and no interrupts during scan-out).

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Measured on boards without PSRAM, and on one with an 8 MB PSRAM fitted on U9 (2026-11-20). Logs and method in docs/rp2350-touch-lcd4.md and docs/log/.

State Display Works. Without PSRAM: 240x240 framebuffer shown as 2x2 pixels, 57.7 fps at 150 MHz, 0 underruns in 1 h and during flash writes. With PSRAM: 480x480, 57.7 fps at 240 MHz (see PSRAM below) LVGL Works. Without PSRAM double buffered (no tearing), pixel output identical to the unix port (64/64 tiles CRC), full-screen redraw 9.2 ms at 150 MHz. With PSRAM one buffer (see below) Touch Works (GT911, LVGL pointer device, no rotation needed). A second unit we have has no touch controller: display_driver then runs without it (display_driver.touch is None) Soft reset, Ctrl-C Work with LVGL running (the scan-out keeps going; LVGL restarts clean) Overclock 200 and 240 MHz tested (PCLK 20 MHz, 76.7 fps), core voltage unchanged. Not the default Backlight PWM, 0–100 % PSRAM (U9, not fitted by Waveshare) Works, detected at boot (APS6404L, 8 MB, CS GPIO47): the GC heap moves to PSRAM (8.2 MB) and the display goes to 480x480 480x480 framebuffer Works with PSRAM: Ctrl-C contract 4 x 60, touch aligned, 30 min soak (see docs/rp2350-touch-lcd4.md). Not possible without PSRAM SD card, CAN (XL2515), RTC, IMU, buzzer, battery Not covered by this port beyond the pin names. RTC (0x51) and IMU (0x6B) answer on I2C1

docs.title: PSRAM and resolution
docs.text:
A 480x480 RGB565 framebuffer is 460 800 B; the RP2350 has 520 KiB of SRAM. The PSRAM footprint (U9) is marked NC on the schematic and is empty on the boards Waveshare ships. The same firmware serves both, and chooses at boot:

Without PSRAM With PSRAM on U9 Framebuffer 240x240 in SRAM, shown as 2x2 pixels 480x480 in SRAM GC heap SRAM, ~330 KB free after import display_driver PSRAM, ~8.2 MB Buffers 2 (no tearing) 1: LVGL draws into the buffer being shown System clock 150 MHz 240 MHz (the PSRAM then runs at 120 MHz) Refresh 57.7 Hz 57.7 Hz

The framebuffer stays in SRAM because the panel's DMA must never wait on the flash/PSRAM bus: any DMA access to it holds the DMA up for 2-4 us, longer than the 16 pixels the PIO FIFO holds, and the picture shifts. With PSRAM the heap therefore leaves SRAM to make room for a 480x480 framebuffer (patches/micropython), and a second 480x480 buffer, which would be in PSRAM, is refused (init(buffers=2) raises MemoryError; display_driver then uses one). MICROPY_HW_RGBPANEL_SCALE 1 or 2 in mpconfigboard.h forces a scale.

Do not use rp2.DMA on PSRAM or flash addresses while the panel runs (at either scale): the panel loses pixels for as long as the transfer lasts. DMA between SRAM buffers and peripherals is fine. With PSRAM, do not change machine.freq(): the PSRAM timing is set for 240 MHz at boot.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Linux x86-64, with git, make, cmake, Python 3 and a host C compiler:

scripts/build_rp2.sh            # → dist/WAVESHARE_RP2350_TOUCH_LCD_4-<commit>.uf2

The script clones MicroPython v1.29.0 and PyDevices omnipython-lvgl (the binding, with LVGL 9.5 as its submodule) at pinned commits into .work/, downloads the xPack arm-none-eabi-gcc 15.2.1-1.1 toolchain (checksum verified) and builds. Running it again reuses everything. WORK_DIR and TOOLCHAIN_DIR override the locations.

By hand, with checkouts of the pinned versions:

LVMP_DIR=/path/to/omnipython-lvgl/ports/micropython \
make -C micropython/ports/rp2 BOARD_DIR=$PWD/boards/rp2/WAVESHARE_RP2350_TOUCH_LCD_4

docs.title: Flash
docs.text:
Hold BOOT, plug USB (or press RESET with BOOT held): the board appears as the RP2350 drive. Copy the .uf2 onto it, or:

picotool load -x WAVESHARE_RP2350_TOUCH_LCD_4-<commit>.uf2

From a running MicroPython: mpremote bootloader, then the same.

The filesystem (12 MiB, LittleFS) starts after the first 4 MiB of flash and is kept across firmware updates.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
import lvgl as lv
import display_driver       # panel, LVGL display, touch, timer: nothing else to call

scr = lv.screen_active()
btn = lv.button(scr)
btn.center()
lv.label(btn).set_text("Hello")

More in examples/ (hello, touch button, animation, backlight, Breakout, Pong, Simon, Snake, tic-tac-toe).

display_driver runs lv.timer_handler() from a 5 ms timer, so a script can end and the UI keeps running (put it in main.py to start at boot). It sets up:

  • display_driver.disp: the LVGL display, WIDTH x HEIGHT (240 x 240, or 480 x 480 with PSRAM), RGB565;
  • display_driver.indev: the GT911 pointer device (None if the touch does not answer);
  • display_driver.stop() / start(): stop/restart the timer, for programs with their own loop calling lv.timer_handler().

Ctrl-C while an LVGL program runs: the first interrupt may stop the LVGL timer instead of the program (a message says so); the next one reaches the program. mpremote sends several, so mpremote run / exec are interrupted normally.

After machine.freq(f) call rgbpanel.init(pclk_hz=...) with a PCLK that divides f / 2 exactly (e.g. 15 MHz at 150 MHz, 20 MHz at 200 or 240 MHz). Otherwise the panel clock follows the system clock and may go out of the panel's range.

docs.title: Memory limits (no PSRAM)
docs.text:
About 190 KB of heap is free after import display_driver; LVGL objects, styles, fonts and images loaded at run time, and the application all share it. LVGL's memory pools take about 26 KB of it (215 KB without them, LVMP_POOLS=none) and keep LVGL's speed the same however fragmented the heap is (docs/rp2350-touch-lcd4.md). Tested with lvgl-mpy-builder output, before the pools: a 3-page, 21-widget UI runs with 205 KB free; its 34-widget "all widgets" test project builds but leaves only ~70 KB free.

Avoid opacity (style_opa < 255), transforms (style_transform_rotation/_scale) and blend modes on large widgets. LVGL draws those through a separate ARGB8888 layer allocated in one piece (4 bytes per pixel of the widget): a 200x150 rotated panel asked for 146 KB. If that allocation fails, LVGL is left half-way through the refresh: the MemoryError is printed, the screen stops updating, and the next change to a widget hangs the board (power cycle needed). This is LVGL/binding behaviour, not specific to this board (docs/upstream/pydevices-issue-oom-render.md); with PSRAM there is more room but the rule stays.

docs.title: rgbpanel (lower level)
docs.text: init(pclk_hz=0, backlight=80, *, buffers=None) start the panel (idempotent; restarts the scan-out if the system clock changed). pclk_hz=0 is 15 MHz. buffers=2 allocates a second framebuffer on the heap (not at 480x480: MemoryError), 1 frees it deinit() stop the scan-out framebuffer(i=0) memoryview ('H', RGB565) of framebuffer i shown(), swap(timeout_ms=100) index of the buffer on screen; show the other one at the end of the frame backlight([percent]) get/set the backlight wait_vsync(timeout_ms=100) wait for the end of the active area frame_count(), underruns(), info() counters and state WIDTH, HEIGHT, SCALE framebuffer size and pixel scale, chosen at boot (480, 480, 1 with PSRAM; 240, 240, 2 without)

docs.title: Resources used
docs.text:
• PIO1 (2 state machines) and PIO2 (2 state machines, all 32 instructions); PIO0 is free for rp2.StateMachine.
  • 3 DMA channels, claimed from the pico-sdk (not visible to rp2.DMA).
  • PWM slice 8 (backlight, GPIO40).
  • SRAM: 123 KB for the static framebuffer and DMA control blocks, 123 KB more on the heap with double buffering. Free heap after import display_driver: ~190 KB.
  • I2C1 (GPIO6/7, 400 kHz) for the touch, shared with RTC and IMU: machine.I2C(1).

docs.title: Pinout
docs.text:
Function GPIO LCD data RGB565 (B1–B5, G0–G5, R1–R5) 24–39 LCD DE / VSYNC / HSYNC / PCLK 20 / 21 / 22 / 23 LCD init SPI (9-bit, bit-banged): CS / SCK / SDA / RST 18 / 2 / 3 / 19 Backlight 40 Touch GT911 (I2C1 0x5D): SDA / SCL / RST / INT 6 / 7 / 16 / 17 RTC PCF85063 (I2C1 0x51) INT 0 IMU QMI8658 (I2C1 0x6B) INT1 / INT2 41 / 42 CAN XL2515 (SPI0): SCK / MOSI / MISO / CS / INT 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 / 44 SD card (SDIO): CLK / CMD / D0–D3 10 / 11 / 12–15 Buzzer 1 Battery CHRG / DONE 42 / 43 (as on the schematic table; GPIO42 is listed twice) UART0 TX / RX (REPL is on USB) 46 / 45 UART1 TX / RX 8 / 9 PSRAM CS (U9) 47

Connector H4 (10 pins): 1 VIN, 2 GND, 3/4 RS485 TX+/TX−, 5/6 CAN L/H, 7 I2C_VCC (3.3 V; 5 V with the H3 solder pad), 8 GND, 9 SDA, 10 SCL. SDA/SCL are I2C1 (GPIO6/7, level shifted), shared with the touch (0x5D), RTC (0x51) and IMU (0x6B). No header has free GPIOs; test pads TP1/TP2 are GPIO46/45 (UART0 TX/RX).

External keyboard: tca8418.py and c64keyboard.py (frozen) drive a TCA8418 keypad controller on H4 with a Commodore 64-style 8x8 matrix, as an LVGL keypad; see examples/c64_keyboard.py. Tested so far against a software model of the chip only.

GPIO2/3 are shared by the LCD init SPI and the CAN controller: initialise CAN after the display (rgbpanel.init() only uses them during the panel init) and keep LCD_CS (GPIO18) high. Names from pins.csv are available as machine.Pin("LCD_BL") etc.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
They run on every board of this repo (the RP2350-Touch-LCD-4 at 240x240, the STM32H743 boards at their panel's size, 1024x600 on the IPS panel) with the same code.

RP2350: run one with mpremote run examples/<name>.py; to start it at power-on copy it to the board as main.py (mpremote cp examples/<name>.py :main.py). STM32H7_CORE V1.3 on the bench (CH340 on UART1, DTR/RTS wired to BOOT0/NRST): python3 scripts/uart_run.py examples/<name>.py (see docs/stm32h743.md).

Example Shows hello.py the minimum: import display_driver, a label, a spinner button.py touch: a button counting taps animation.py LVGL animations (no tearing: double buffered) backlight.py a slider setting the backlight with display_driver.backlight() (on/off on the STM32 boards for now) c64_keyboard.py typing on a C64-style keyboard (TCA8418 on connector H4 of the RP2350 board, see python/c64keyboard.py); without it, says so breakout.py a game: drag the paddle, break the bricks (ball physics in an LVGL timer, buzzer if the board has one) pong.py a game: you against the microcontroller, drag your paddle up and down simon.py a game: repeat the growing sequence of colours (LVGL timer, buzzer if the board has one) snake.py a game: snake controlled by tapping on the side to turn to (LVGL objects reused as segments) tictactoe.py a game: you (X) against the microcontroller (O, minimax: it never loses) shell/ a Linux-like shell on the screen, keyboard from a terminal on the serial port: files, pipes, wildcards, history, Tab; with vi and a friendlier edit, and an ANSI terminal module for your own programs. The font in ansifont.py is under the SIL OFL. Goes in / (shell.py, ansiterm.py, ansifont.py) and /bin (vi.py, edit.py), then import shell; shell.main(). On the RP2350 (no PSRAM) copy shell, ansiterm and ansifont compiled with mpy-cross (.mpy): compiled on the board they leave too little heap for the terminal's 115 KB framebuffer (MemoryError) weather.py ESP32-4848S040 only: weather, wind and 5 days of forecast from Open-Meteo, with drawn icons, setup on the touchscreen and settings on the SD card home/ ESP32-4848S040 only: the shell at power-on and a touch menu of apps (weather, games, Copper and Code Studio apps), each started alone after a reset; everything on the SD card but main.py

Any resolution: sizes are written for a 240 px display and scaled with ui.px(n) (python/ui.py: n times the shorter side / 240, so unchanged on the RP2350 board), fonts with ui.font(size) (the closest Montserrat compiled in: 14, 16, 24, 32, 40), positions from display_driver.WIDTH / HEIGHT or LVGL alignment. Game speeds scale with ui.UNIT too; the breakout wall and the snake field get more columns on a wide display. Sound goes through python/buzzer.py (GPIO1 on the RP2350 board; silent where there is no buzzer, as on the STM32 boards so far).

Every example ends after building its screen: display_driver keeps LVGL running from a timer. mpremote (or, on the STM32 bench, opening the serial port) resets the board before each run, so running another example replaces the previous one. Ctrl-C works as usual in programs with their own loop.

docs.title: A printable box for the RP2350-Touch-LCD-4
docs.text:
Not printed yet: the fit is untested. A box for the Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-4: the board sits on four standoffs, the display's bezel rests in a ledge at the top.

File make_box.py the parametric model, in CadQuery RP2350_Touch_LCD_4_Box.stl for the slicer RP2350_Touch_LCD_4_Box.step for a CAD program

Outside about 89.4 x 89.4 x 18 mm, corners rounded at 3 mm. Inside:

  • a 2 mm ledge for the 84.2 x 84.2 mm bezel, 0.4 mm of play;
  • a 76.5 x 78.5 mm cavity, 14 mm deep, for the 74.5 x 76.5 mm PCB;
  • four standoffs 66.5 x 68.5 mm apart, with 2.3 mm holes for M2.5 self-tapping screws (3.2 mm for M2 heat-set inserts: change hole_d);
  • an opening at the bottom for the green terminal block, and a slot on the left side for the USB-C, the microSD and the RST/BOOT buttons.

The board dimensions come from Waveshare's dimension drawing for the board (wiki); the drawing itself is Waveshare's and is not copied here.

docs.title: Changing it
docs.text:
The parameters are at the top of make_box.py (tolerance, walls, floor, depth, holes). Then:

pip install cadquery
python3 make_box.py      # writes the .stl and .step into the current folder

docs.title: To check on the first print
docs.text:
• The side slot is centred on the face. usbc_center_y, the USB-C's height from the drawing, is computed but not used yet: on a print, check that the slot is over the USB-C, the card and the buttons, or move it there.
  • The 0.4 mm play suits a 0.4 mm nozzle; tighter printers may need less.
